title: Where you belong
hook: people choose a community by warmth, practice and place

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: visit. Going in as a learner and a guest. Which service did you put on your calendar? Today, the question a visit can raise: where do I stay? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

The real estate agent has shown the kitchen, the yard and the closets. Then the couple asks a question she didn't expect: how long is the walk to the synagogue? They don't drive on Shabbat, so the shul they choose will help decide the street they live on, and the street will help decide the shul. Other families ask other first questions. Who will know our names? Will the prayers sound like the ones we grew up with? Each answer is a piece of the same choice. Today is about how people choose where they belong.
screen: `HOW FAR IS THE WALK?` → `THE STREET AND THE SHUL.` → `WHO WILL KNOW OUR NAMES?`

segments.voice: Where you belong. Turn it four ways. First, warmth. Ask people why they joined their synagogue, and the answer is sometimes a person. Someone greeted them by name the second time they came. Someone brought soup when the baby was born. The rabbi remembered their father's name. People sometimes follow a face before they follow a platform. Second, practice. A community has to fit the way you live. Is the prayer in Hebrew or in English, fast or slow? Do men and women sit together? How is Shabbat kept, and how strictly is that expected of you? A warm room that asks for a life you don't want to live, or doesn't make room for the life you do, can be hard to stay in. Third, place. For Jews who don't drive on Shabbat, the synagogue has to be within walking distance, so where they live and where they pray decide each other. For others, place means a commute, a city, or a screen. Fourth, the teaching that sits underneath. In the Mishnah, Joshua ben Perachiah says: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend. Make, and acquire: both are things you do. He doesn't say which teacher or which friend. Some people find their place on the first try. Some change places as their lives change: a student group, a young family's synagogue, a quiet minyan in old age. Some belong to two. The tradition's pressure is not toward one right answer. It is toward having a teacher and a friend somewhere, people you can call my people.
screen: `WARMTH: A FACE BEFORE A PLATFORM.` · `PRACTICE: A FIT FOR YOUR LIFE.` · `PLACE: WHERE YOU CAN WALK.` · `MAKE A TEACHER, ACQUIRE A FRIEND.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU BELONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on your community. Settle, and breathe. Name the people you would call my people: a synagogue, a church, a family, a team, a few friends, or nobody yet. Take the three questions one at a time. Warmth: who there knows your name? Practice: does it fit the way you live, or ask you to hide part of it? Place: can you actually get there? Don't decide anything. Just notice where the answers are strong and where they are thin. If you pray, you can bring that picture into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Where you belong. A community chosen by warmth, practice and place, where you can make a teacher and acquire a friend. Today's word.
Your line: where you belong. Today, do one thing that ties you a little tighter to your people: a call, a visit, a name learned. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews choose a synagogue or community by its people, its practice and its location; those who walk on Shabbat live within walking distance of the synagogue they attend.

warmth, practice and place, and a teacher and a friend.
